title: What to know about Anthropic’s ‘Claude-led’ biological discovery — and why scientists aren’t convinced
key_facts: Anthropic said last month that AI agents at its biology lab found an unusual DNA pattern in viruses, a "novel enzyme system" it suspects could be a new gene editing mechanism.
Anthropic says 950 AI agents spent 21 hours searching DNA data, picking out 3,500 reverse transcriptase enzymes and narrowing to 20.
Experts not involved call the finding early and incremental; the work is not peer reviewed and what the sequences do is not determined.
Mario Rodríguez Mestre, who used Claude for his University of Copenhagen doctoral research, says his unpublished research describes the same viral signatures.
He says he is not claiming Anthropic deliberately took his work and cannot demonstrate it.
MIT's Feng Zhang called the work "genuinely intriguing" in an Anthropic release.
Shares of gene-editing companies fell shortly after the announcement, per CNN.
quote_evidence: “These are very interesting preliminary results, but at this point they don’t demonstrate gene editing or provide a mechanistic picture of exactly what’s happening,” said Aaron Engelhart, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota’s Department of Genetics, Cell Biology, and Development.
“I am not claiming that Anthropic deliberately took our work. I cannot demonstrate that,” he told CNN via email.
why_it_matters_hint: A headline AI-science claim is contested on both its significance and its credit, and researchers may think twice about feeding unpublished work to AI tools.
event_date: Anthropic announcement last month (exact date not stated); CNN report 8 Oct 2026
notes: Date of the original Anthropic announcement and of Mestre's claim are not given in the article.
